title: Cocaine killed woman
article: A Harrowsmith woman, who died less than four hours after she was arrested in February, succumbed to "an enormous over-dose of cocaine," an inquest was told yesterday.

Dr. Marco Sivilotti, the doctor who tried to revive Susan Maleska after she arrived at Kingston General Hospital on Feb. 24, testified that he doesn't believe there was anything more that he or the paramedics who first attended Maleska could have done to save her.
Sivilotti, an expert in emergency medicine and toxicology, said the care she received from paramedics was "absolutely exemplary."
Jurors learned that a baggie of cocaine was found in Maleska's throat. Sivilotti said the cocaine continued to enter her system as she was dying.
Det. Const. Craig Smith, a member of the local drug enforcement unit, told the inquest that he was the first police officer to have contact with the 44-year-old Maleska, at 1:33 a.m.
He was one of five officers who had gone to the Rutledge Road farm house of William Day to execute a drug warrant.
Smith said he found Maleska about 15 seconds after entering the house. She was sitting on a bed with a deck of cards and appeared to be playing solitaire, he recalled.

He told the inquest her hands were always in his view. When he asked her if there was anyone else in the house with her she told him, "not that I'm aware of." She gave the same response when he asked her if there were drugs in the house and insisted, "I don't do drugs, I can promise you that."
She also told Smith that she'd only been staying at the farm for two and a half days.
While he remained with Maleska, Smith testified, officers found Day in the basement and he asked Maleska to get dressed. She was wearing only a T-shirt and boxer shorts.
He said he checked her socks for hidden items and asked her to turn out her pockets in front of him, which disclosed one small blue pill, which Maleska identified as morphine.

She told him it was for chronic back pain. Smith said he searched through her purse where he found a small pill bottle with no label containing an assortment of pills and an Altoids tin holding a razor blade and two small lumps of resin "which she identified as hashish."
He concluded from the drugs in her purse and her disclosures that she used drugs, "but at no time did I think she was under the influence," he told jurors.
Smith said he put handcuffs on Maleska and removed her from the house, placing her in one of the cruisers after she began interrupting another officer's attempts to question Day.
The OPP officer who drove Maleska to the South Frontenac OPP detachment also recalled nothing that suggested to him she was in any kind of physical distress or under the influence of drugs.
Const. Peter Robb said he found her already seated in another cruiser when he arrived at the farm at 2:16 a.m., and he helped her out of that car.

Before transporting her, Robb said he asked if Maleska had been searched and was assured that she had. He told the inquest that she walked to his cruiser "under her own power," and after they arrived in the detachment booking area, 12 minutes later, she removed her own jewelry and belt without difficulty.
There was no tape of her booking. Robb and Const. Buff Chadwick both told the inquest they didn't initially hear an alarm that signalled the tape needed to be replaced.
Consequently, the tape that inquest jurors were shown begins after Maleska was placed in a cell that's normally used for youths.
Between 2:51 and 2:52 a.m. the tape captures her walking to the back of the cell, where she climbs onto a cot and slips under a white blanket.
Three minutes later, the blanket jumps near her feet several times and within a minute her spasming is pronounced and becoming more forceful.
The tape captures Robb and Chadwick entering the cell, by which time Maleska is fully convulsing, her legs flailing, feet arched unnaturally and toes pointed.
The inquest was told she stopped convulsing - and breathing - just as paramedics arrived at 3:16 a.m., but efforts to revive her continued for another 92 minutes.
The inquest continues this morning at the Frontenac County Court House.
